section: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: A Phrase, a Philosophy, and a Historical Debate
text:
Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: A Phrase, a Philosophy, and a Historical Debate
The phrase “standing on the shoulders of giants” is one of the most famous expressions of intellectual humility and gratitude. It reminds us that progress in science, education, and knowledge is never created in isolation but builds upon the discoveries and insights of those who came before us.

title: The Physics Teacher
text:
The Origin and Meaning
The phrase is most famously attributed to Isaac Newton, who wrote in a letter to Robert Hooke in 1675:

“If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.”

Newton was acknowledging that his breakthroughs were possible because of the foundational work done by earlier scientists like Galileo, Kepler, and Hooke himself. The metaphor conveys the idea that we can see further—understand more—when we build on the vast achievements of past thinkers.
However, this phrase was not coined by Newton. It has medieval roots, appearing as early as the 12th century with the philosopher Bernard of Chartres, who likened scholars to dwarfs perched on the shoulders of giants, able to see more and farther than they could on their own.

title: The Physics Teacher
section: Teaching and Science: A Shared Tradition
text:
Teaching and Science: A Shared Tradition
In physics teaching, this phrase carries special weight. Demonstrations, experiments, and explanations we use today are the result of centuries of collective insight and innovation. By sharing these with students, we pass on not only facts but a lineage of curiosity, discovery, and wonder.

title: The Physics Teacher
section: The Newton-Hooke Rivalry: Was It a Slur?
text:
The Newton-Hooke Rivalry: Was It a Slur?
The phrase’s context is sometimes viewed through a more contentious lens. Newton’s relationship with Robert Hooke was complicated—marked by moments of cooperation but also rivalry and disagreement over scientific credit.
Some have speculated that Newton’s phrase was a subtle dig at Hooke. Their reasoning includes:

Hooke’s Physical Stature: Hooke was reportedly short and possibly physically deformed, which leads some to interpret the saying as a veiled short-joke at Hooke’s expense. Given their clashes over priority and ideas, the compliment might have been sarcastic.
Newton’s Other Correspondence: Newton was very dismissive, insulting and, cold towards Hooke elsewhere.


But What Does the Evidence Say?
Most historians disagree with the idea that Newton was insulting Hooke with this phrase. Instead, they point out:

The metaphor was a common expression of humility and respect well before Newton.
The full letter shows Newton acknowledging Hooke’s important contributions.
There is no explicit insult or mocking language in the letter.
Newton acknowledged other giants openly and genuinely.

In fact, the phrase fits more as a respectful nod to the continuum of knowledge rather than a veiled slur.

title: The Physics Teacher
text:
Why Does It Matter?
It doesn’t specially - but understanding what was meant by “standing on the shoulders of giants” helps us appreciate the collaborative nature of science. It reminds educators and students alike that learning is a shared journey. Each new insight, each “aha” moment, is built on a foundation laid by others.
Rather than focusing on personal rivalries, the phrase encourages humility, gratitude, and inspiration to push the boundaries further.

title: The Physics Teacher
text:
Final Thoughts
Whether in the lecture theatre, the lab, or the classroom, the spirit of standing on the shoulders of giants invites us to see beyond ourselves and to contribute, one day, to the shoulders upon which future generations will stand.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.1 Introduction
phyphox (pronounced “fee-focks”) stands for Physical Phone Experiments. It is a free mobile app designed to transform your smartphone into a powerful physics laboratory. Developed by researchers at RWTH Aachen University in Germany, phyphox leverages the multitude of sensors embedded in modern smartphones—such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, magnetometers, barometers, microphones, and cameras—to perform real-time physics experiments.
Since its launch, phyphox has become an invaluable tool for educators, students, and enthusiasts around the world, enabling hands-on learning that is accessible, versatile, and engaging.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.2 Why phyphox?
Smartphones are ubiquitous, and their built-in sensors are sophisticated enough to measure physical phenomena with surprising accuracy. phyphox harnesses these capabilities by providing easy-to-use experimental setups that require minimal additional equipment. This democratizes physics experimentation by removing traditional barriers like expensive lab gear or dedicated sensors.
Key advantages include:

Accessibility: Available for free on both Android and iOS.
Portability: Experiments can be done anywhere—classrooms, outdoors, or at home.
Interactivity: Real-time data visualization and analysis within the app.
Flexibility: Customizable experiments and exportable raw data for further study.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.3 Core Features

1.3.1 1. Sensor-Based Experiments
phyphox offers dozens of predefined experiments using smartphone sensors, including:

Accelerometer: Measure acceleration, free fall, pendulum motion, or vibrations.
Gyroscope: Analyze rotational motion and angular velocity.
Magnetometer: Detect magnetic fields, measure Earth’s magnetic flux density.
Barometer: Investigate pressure changes, altitude, and weather-related phenomena.
Microphone: Study sound waves, frequency analysis, and resonance.
Light Sensor & Camera: Explore optics, light intensity, and color analysis.
Proximity Sensor: Time-of-flight measurements and simple motion detection.



1.3.2 2. Real-Time Data Display and Processing

Live graphs and numerical data display.
Basic data analysis functions like integration, differentiation, and Fourier transform.
Adjustable sampling rates and data smoothing.
Customizable experiment parameters.



1.3.3 3. Data Export and Sharing
phyphox allows exporting data in standard formats such as CSV, facilitating deeper analysis using spreadsheet software or scientific tools like Python, MATLAB, or Excel.


1.3.4 4. Custom Experiments
Users with technical skills can create or modify experiments using the phyphox experiment file format—a simple XML-based configuration that defines sensors, data processing, and user interface elements. This flexibility supports educators and researchers in tailoring experiments to specific learning goals.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.4 Example Experiments
Here are some common experiments you can perform with phyphox:

Simple Pendulum: Using the accelerometer, measure period and damping.
Free Fall: Drop the phone safely and verify acceleration due to gravity.
Roller Coaster Analysis: Record acceleration and forces experienced during rides.
Sound Frequency Analysis: Capture and analyze sound waves and resonance frequencies.
Magnetic Field Mapping: Map spatial variations in magnetic fields using the magnetometer.
Barometric Altitude: Track altitude changes when climbing stairs or hills.
Rotational Dynamics: Study spinning motions and angular velocities.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:
1.5 Applications in Education
phyphox fits perfectly into physics education at many levels:

Hands-On Learning: Students perform real experiments rather than only simulations or theory.
Inquiry-Based Teaching: Encourages hypothesis, measurement, data analysis, and interpretation.
Cost-Effective Labs: Removes the need for expensive dedicated sensors.
Remote or Hybrid Learning: Supports experimentation outside of traditional classrooms.
Cross-Disciplinary Connections: Links physics to technology, engineering, and data science.

Teachers can integrate phyphox into their lesson plans easily. For example, when teaching kinematics, students can measure acceleration during a walk or in a car; when discussing waves, they can analyze sound frequencies or light intensities.

title: 1  Phy-Phox: Physics Phone Experiments
text:

Supported Platforms: Android (Google Play Store) and iOS (Apple App Store).
Device Requirements: Modern smartphones with the relevant sensors (most devices made in the last 5–7 years).
Cost: Free with no ads or in-app purchases.
Languages: Available in multiple languages, including English, German, Spanish, and more.

title: 2  PhET Interactive Simulations: Bringing Physics to Life

2.1 Introduction
PhET Interactive Simulations is a project developed by the University of Colorado Boulder that offers free, high-quality, research-based interactive simulations for teaching and learning science and mathematics. Since its inception in 2002, PhET has become a leading resource worldwide, providing engaging, accessible digital tools that help students visualize and explore complex scientific concepts.
PhET simulations cover physics, chemistry, biology, earth science, and math, making it a versatile platform for educators and learners of all ages.

2.2 Why PhET?
PhET’s core mission is to make science accessible and exciting through interactive, inquiry-based learning. Unlike traditional static textbooks or lectures, PhET simulations provide dynamic environments where students can manipulate variables, observe outcomes in real time, and develop deeper conceptual understanding.
Key benefits include:

Interactive Learning: Engage students actively by letting them explore phenomena instead of passively receiving information.
Research-Based Design: Developed with input from education researchers to promote effective learning.
Free and Open Access: All simulations are freely available online and offline.
Cross-Platform: Available on web browsers and mobile devices without needing downloads or installations.
Multilingual Support: Simulations are translated into multiple languages, broadening accessibility.

title: 3  Basic Physics
text:
3.2 Stories to enritch

3.2.1 The Mars Climate Orbiter Crash





In 1999, NASA lost a $125 million spacecraft because of a simple mistake: one team used imperial units while the other used metric. A force calculated in pound-seconds was interpreted as newton-seconds. The result? The probe entered Mars’ atmosphere at the wrong angle and was destroyed. It’s a dramatic reminder that units really do matter — in space, there are no second chances.


3.2.2 Fermi’s Paper Trick
At the first nuclear test in 1945, physicist Enrico Fermi dropped pieces of paper as the shockwave hit. By estimating how far they moved, he calculated the energy of the explosion — within a factor of two of the actual value. With no instruments, just logic and estimation, he showed how powerful order-of-magnitude thinking can be.


3.2.3 Drag, Planes, and Pi
Before computers or wind tunnels, scientists wanted to understand what affects drag on an object. Using only dimensional analysis, they figured out how drag must depend on speed, fluid density, and surface area. This led to the discovery of the Reynolds number — a key idea in fluid dynamics. It all came from playing with units and looking for dimensionless combinations.


3.2.4 Galileo Rolls the Ball





Galileo rolled balls down a ramp and timed them with a water clock. He noticed the distance didn’t increase steadily — it grew faster and faster. He realized distance was proportional to time squared. It was one of the first steps toward understanding acceleration and laid the foundation for Newton’s laws — all from careful observation and simple timing.


3.2.5 Maxwell’s Speed of Light
In the 1800s, James Clerk Maxwell found that the speed of electromagnetic waves could be calculated from two physical constants. When he worked it out, the speed matched that of light. Suddenly, light wasn’t just a mystery — it was a wave in electric and magnetic fields. Units helped reveal one of the most profound connections in physics.
From Maxwell’s equations in vacuum (no charges, no currents), we can derive the wave equations for the electric and magnetic fields. Note that this is just for fun and is wayyy above A-Level:
\[
\nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}
\]
\[
\nabla^2 \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{B}}{\partial t^2}
\]
where:

( \(\mu_0\)) = permeability of free space
( \(\epsilon_0\) ) = permittivity of free space

The general form of a wave equation is:
\[ \nabla^2 \psi = \frac{1}{v^2} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} \]
where ( v ) is the wave speed.
Comparing forms:
\[ \nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = \mu_{0} \epsilon_{0} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2} \]
we identify:
\[ v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \epsilon_0}} \]
Since these are the equations for electromagnetic waves:
\[ \boxed{c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \epsilon_0}}} \]

Constants
\[ \mu_0 = 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \text{H/m} \]
\[ \epsilon_0 \approx 8.854187817 \times 10^{-12} \text{F/m} \]
Substituting:
\[ c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{ (4 \pi \times 10^{-7}) \times (8.854187817 \times 10^{-12}) }} \]
\[ =\boxed{299{,}792{,}458 \ \text{m/s}} \]



3.2.6 How many tools does it take…
… To change a lightbulb? Two if you are in the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS was built by an international consortium which fostered collaboration but also led to some practical quirks. The modules built by the United States are made using Imperial units and fasteners, whilst the European, Russian and Japanese modules use the metric versions. Both metric and imperial tools have to be available for the astronauts.


3.2.7 Banana equivalent dose
A unit used to provide an everyday measure of radiation dose. A single banana produces an ionising radiation dose of around 0.1 μSv which has been set as the value of the banana equivalent dose. The ionising radiation dose given by a range of sources can be expressed in BEDs. A Dental X-ray has a dose of 50 Bananas.


3.2.8 The Smoot





In 1958, Oliver R. Smoot, an MIT freshman, became an unlikely part of measurement history — and the basis of one of the most delightfully absurd units in physics: the smoot.
As part of a fraternity prank, Smoot’s brothers decided to measure the length of the Harvard Bridge (between Boston and Cambridge) using Smoot himself as the ruler. They had him lie down on the sidewalk, mark his position, then repeat — all the way across the bridge.
The final measurement? \(364.4\text{ smoots} \pm 1\text{ ear}\).
Yes — they even included an uncertainty estimate. The “ear” was the estimated margin of error based on Smoot’s slight squirming or misalignment during the process.

text:
3.3 Practical work and Demos

3.3.1 Estimates of quantities
It is always important in Physics to have a rough idea of the values of quantities that you are attempting to measure. Introduce this idea by a set of intelligent guesses and fermi problems.
Fermi problems are estimation challenges named after physicist Enrico Fermi, who was known for making good approximate calculations with little or no actual data. These problems involve breaking down complex questions into simpler parts, making reasonable assumptions, and using estimation and logic to arrive at an approximate answer.
A classic example is: “How many piano tuners are there in Chicago?” To solve this, you’d estimate the population of Chicago, how many households might have pianos, how often they’re tuned, and how many tunings one person can do — then work your way to a rough answer.
Fermi problems develop skills in:

Critical thinking
Problem decomposition
Reasonable estimation
Handling orders of magnitude
They’re often used in science and engineering education to build confidence in tackling big or unfamiliar questions with limited data.

Having a physical sense of measurements can be very advantageous - especially in preparation for practical examinations (international exams only at time of writing). Try getting the students to:

guess the temperature of hot water (at about 50) in a bucket by feel
time 30s with eyes closed by counting against the clock.
the length of the lab just by looking at it
the height of a tree outside
the number of bricks in the wall of the lab

A really good demo for this is

Measuring Cylinders of Different Diameters

Setup:
Two measuring cylinders, one with twice the diameter of the other. Pour a certain volume from the larger into the smaller.


Question:
How high will the liquid be in the smaller cylinder?


Answer:

4 times higher, if diameter ratio is 2:1.
Great for pointing out the use of ratio and fractions even in qualatative questions.



Variant: Two martini glasses

Setup:
Fill two martini glasses to 1/2 their volume full of water or any other liquid. They will look 3/4 full.


Question:
What will happen when one is emptied into the other?


Answer:
The glass fills exactly to it’s full height - a very suprising lesson in shape volume.

3.3.2 Dimensional analysis
Dimensional analysis is a powerful method used in science and engineering to check equations, derive relationships, and convert between units. It’s based on the principle that physical quantities must be dimensionally consistent — meaning both sides of an equation must have the same basic units (such as mass \(M\), length \(L\), time \(T\), etc.).
For example, speed has dimensions of distance divided by time, \(D/T \text{ or } DT^{-1}\). If you’re given an equation involving speed, distance, and time, dimensional analysis can help you verify if it’s physically meaningful.
Key uses of dimensional analysis include:

Checking equations for consistency
Deriving formulas when the exact relationship isn’t known
Converting units (e.g. km/h to m/s)
Estimating outcomes in physics problems

It’s a valuable tool for spotting errors and making sense of unfamiliar problems using just the units involved.


3.3.3 Getting values for the sizes of small quantities
The sizes of small measurements (mass or length) can best be found by measuring a large number of the objects and then dividing the result by the number of objects. This technique is one of the few that reduces uncertainty.
For example:
The thickness of a sheet of paper is best found by measuring the thickness of a number of sheets. if 10 of them are found to be 1.10mm \(\pm\) 0.01mm then the thickness is 0.11mm \(\pm\) 0.001mm.
The volume of a marble can be accurately found by measuring the diameter of five of them in a line.
The mass of a single small ball bearing can be found by measuring the mass of a known large number of them.

3.3.5 Measuring Distance Accurately
In the course of learning physics students need to learn the art of precision measurements. Use a variety of measuring instruments (Metre ruler, Vernier caliper, Micrometer) to measure small objects (e.g., pencil, bolt). Try not to use tools with a digital readout until the concept of a vernier scale is solidly understood.
There’s a great model of a micrometer here and a vernier caliper here
The concepts of precision, scale reading, and significant figures are critical. Have students measure the same object with ruler, caliper, and micrometer.
Discuss:

Zero error - the error that occurs when a measuring instrument shows a reading other than zero when it should actually read zero.



Precision - Precision refers to how closely repeated measurements of the same quantity agree with each other.
Uncertainty - Uncertainty is an estimate of the range within which the true value of a measured quantity is expected to err, and…

3.3.6 Stopwatch Reaction Time
Human reaction time is only accurate to about \(\pm 0.3s\). You can explore this effectively with the ruler drop test.

One person holds the ruler vertically so that:


The 0 cm mark is at the bottom.
The ruler is positioned between the thumb and forefinger of the catcher, but not touching.


The catcher gets ready, with their fingers open.
Without warning, the holder releases the ruler.
The catcher closes their fingers as quickly as possible to catch the ruler.
Record the measurement on the ruler at the point where it was caught (this is the distance fallen).

Use the equation of motion for free fall:
\[
s=1/2gt^{2}
\]
where:

s = distance the ruler fell (m)
g = acceleration due to gravity (≈ 9.81 m/s²)
t= reaction time (s)

Rearrange:
\[t=\sqrt{\frac{2s}{g}}\]​​

3.3.8 Water Displacement for Volume





Over 2,000 years ago, in ancient Greece, the king asked Archimedes to solve a problem: Was his new crown made of pure gold — or had the goldsmith cheated by mixing in cheaper metals?
Archimedes thought hard, but couldn’t figure out how to test it without damaging the crown. One day, while lowering himself into a full bath, he noticed the water overflowed. At that moment, he realised:

An object displaces its own volume of water. He had found a way to measure the crown’s volume — without melting it.

Excited, he jumped out of the bath and ran through the streets shouting:

“Eureka!” or “I have found it!”

Using water displacement to find the volume of irregular objects is a fantastic opportunity to teach how to measure volume and parallax error etc.

Fill the displacement can:
Fill the can with water until water just starts to flow out of the spout. Wait until it stops dripping — the can is now full to the spout level.
Place a measuring cylinder under the spout.
Make sure it’s ready to catch any displaced water.
Gently lower the object into the can.

Make sure no water splashes out (that would give error).
Ensure the object is completely submerged.

Collect the displaced water in the cylinder.
The water that overflows equals the volume of the object.
Read the volume of water collected.
This is the volume of the object (since: \(\text{volume of object} = \text{volume of displaced water}\) )
Example: If the measuring cylinder shows: \(75 \ \text{ml}\) then the volume of the object is \(75 \ \text{cm}^3\)

title: 4  Work, Energy, & Power
text:
4.1 Work, Energy, and Power: Basic Theory
General theory for this section:

title: 4  Work, Energy, & Power
text:
4.1.1 Work (\(W\))

Work is done when a force causes displacement: \[
W = F d \cos \theta
\] Where:
\(F\) = applied force (N)
\(d\) = displacement (m)
\(\theta\) = angle between force and displacement
Units: joules (J), where \(1\,\text{J} = 1\,\text{N·m}\)
No work is done if there is:

No displacement
Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g. circular motion)




4.1.2 Energy

Energy is the capacity to do work.


Kinetic Energy (\(E_k\))

Energy of a moving object: \[
E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2
\] Where \(m\) is mass (kg) and \(v\) is speed (m/s)



Gravitational Potential Energy (\(E_p\))

Energy due to position in a gravitational field: \[
E_p = m g h
\] Where \(g = 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\) (on Earth), \(h\) is height (m)



Elastic Potential Energy

Stored in stretched/compressed springs: \[
E = \frac{1}{2} k x^2
\] Where \(k\) is spring constant (N/m), \(x\) is extension/compression (m)




4.1.3 Conservation of Energy

Total energy is conserved in a closed system: \[
\text{Total energy in} = \text{Total energy out}
\]
Energy can be transformed (e.g. potential ↔︎ kinetic) but not created or destroyed.



4.1.4 Power (\(P\))

Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: \[
P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{E}{t}
\] Where:
\(W\) = work done (J)
\(t\) = time (s)
Units: watts (W), where \(1\,\text{W} = 1\,\text{J/s}\)



4.1.5 Alternative expressions:

If an object is moving at constant speed under constant force: \[
P = F v
\]



4.1.6 Efficiency

A measure of how much input energy is usefully transferred: \[
\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{input energy}} \times 100\%
\]

title: 4  Work, Energy, & Power
text:
4.2 Stories to enrich

4.2.1 Hero’s Steam Engine: The First Work Done by Steam





Though called Hero’s engine, Vitruvius’s (c. 80 BC – c. 15 BC) was the first to mention aeolipiles by name:

Aeolipilae are hollow brazen vessels, which have an opening or mouth of small size, by means of which they can be filled with water. Prior to the water being heated over the fire, but little wind is emitted. As soon, however, as the water begins to boil, a violent wind issues forth.[6]

Hero (c. 10–70 AD) takes a more practical approach, in that he gives instructions how to make one:

PLACE a cauldron over a fire: a ball shall revolve on a pivot. A fire is ignited under a cauldron, A B, (fig. 50), containing water, and covered at the mouth by the lid C D; with this the bent tube E F G communicates, the extremity of the tube being fitted into a hollow ball, H K. Opposite to the extremity G place a pivot, L M, resting on the lid C D; and let the ball contain two bent pipes, communicating with it at the opposite extremities of a diameter, and bent in opposite directions, the bends being at right angles and across the lines F G, L M. As the cauldron gets hot it will be found that the steam, entering the ball through E F G, passes out through the bent tubes towards the lid, and causes the ball to revolve, as in the case of the dancing figures.

Rather oddly it appears that nobody thought to do anything with these machines for centuries after this. Their main use appears to have been a curio displayed in temples.


4.2.2 James Joule’s Honeymoon
James Joule, whose name we use for the unit of energy, was so passionate about energy conservation that he ran an experiment on his honeymoon. While visiting the Alps in 1847, Joule measured the temperature rise of water at the bottom of a waterfall, testing whether the mechanical energy of the falling water converted to heat. His findings supported the idea that mechanical work and heat were two forms of the same thing — energy. His new bride, according to some accounts, may not have been quite as enthusiastic about the experiment.


4.2.3 James Watt and the Horsepower Revolution
James Watt improved the steam engine in the 18th century and coined the term horsepower to describe engine power relative to draft horses. His work transformed energy from a natural force into a measurable quantity used in industry. This idea helped quantify how much work engines could do, fueling the Industrial Revolution. His improvements were so successful that, along with his commercial partner, Watt quickly built a thriving company that supplied steam-driven pumps to mines.
Amusingly the volume of paperwork he was faced with increased hugely and Watt struggled to find enough clerks to copy the documents of buisness. He did what any frustrated inventor would do and, along with Joseph Black, Watt invented the first copier.
The first copy of a document was written in a gelatinous ink which was then dampened and pressed against another thin sheet by passing the two documents between two rollers. Tough the copy was only legible if read through the back of the copied sheet it produced a usable “photocopy”. Watt patented the device and sold 200 of the copiers in their first year of manufacture including a number to Thomas Jefferson


4.2.4 The Falling Weight: Joule’s Paddle Wheel Experiment
James Prescott Joule carefully measured how much work was done by falling weights to stir water, observing temperature changes. This experiment linked mechanical work with heat energy, laying the foundation for the conservation of energy principle. It showed that energy could be transformed but not destroyed.
The paddle-wheel experiment seems to be straightforward, but attempts to replicate it from Joule’s methodological description highlight either his prowess as an experimental scientist or his talents for inventive description. Joule’s instructions require an experimenter to use pulleys to raise and then drop two 13 kg masses 20 times within a 35-minute period. Between each winding, the experimenter must pause to take temperature readings from behind a wooden shield to prevent heating by their body affecting the experiment.
His gravestone, in Sale, Greater Manchester, has the number 772.55 engraved on it, the magnitude of work required to heat a pound of water by one degree in foot-pounds.







4.2.5 The Boiling Amazon
For hundreds of years, legends spoke of a boiling river in the Amazonian jungle. In 2011, geoscientist Andrés Ruzo rediscovered and began studying the river. The average temperature of the water is 86°C and is heated by hot springs powered by geological fault lines.



4.2.6 The Human Body: A Power Plant
The average human at rest produces about 100 watts of power—roughly the same as a light bulb. But a sprinter can output over 1,000 watts in a short burst. Our bodies convert chemical energy from food into mechanical work and heat. Understanding this helped develop sports science and ergonomics.

4.3 Practical work and Demos

4.3.1 Cars and carpet
One of the misconceptions that appears commonly is the need to push an object to cause it to move, as opposed to accelerating it. This comes about principally due to our experience of everything suffering friction. A very nice demonstration of work done against friction is in the braking of a toy car or trolley as it rolls down a ramp on to a piece of carpet. By measuring the stopping distance, and the energy involved, one can find the braking force. This can be done by either measuring the loss of potential energy as it runs down the ramp and on to the carpet or finding the loss of kinetic energy by measuring its speed with a light gate as it reaches the carpet.
Simmilar things can be done by comparing the height drop of the cresta-run with the final velocity of the sledders. In many parts of the UK you’ll see escape lanes filled with gravel at the sides of steep hills to stop runaway traffic. There are some spectacular videos of these in action on youtube.

For a car of mass m travelling down a ramp from a height h and reaching a speed v at the bottom:
Loss of kinetic energy as it brakes to a stop on the carpet = Braking force (F) x Braking distance (d)
Potential energy lost in travelling down the ramp = mgh
If we assume that this is all converted to kinetic energy then mgh = Fd
If we use the velocity and therefore the kinetic energy at the base of the ramp then we can ignore the effect of friction on the the ramp.
\[ \text{Kinetic energy} = 1/2 mv^{2} = Fd\]

4.3.3 Are you more powerful than Yoda?
The core of this investiagation is a classic experiment to measure a pupil’s power - they carry their own mass (themselves) up a known height. The pupils run up a flight of stairs of known height and measure the time that they take to do it. They then can measure their own weight or use “the international standard physicist mass1” of 80Kg and so calculate the work done and the power that they developed. Carrying a rucksack loaded with books will increase their weight.
The second part of this was inspired by the wonderful https://what-if.xkcd.com/3/. In turn that was inspired by the great SMBC comic exploring the geopolitical consequences of having Superman turn a crank to provide an unlimited source of energy.
Yoda’s greatest display of raw power in the original trilogy came when he lifted Luke’s X-Wing from the swamp. As far as physically moving objects around goes, this was easily the biggest expenditure of energy through the Force we saw from anyone in the trilogy.
I tend to walk the students through the following fermi-problem:
The energy it takes to lift an object to height h is equal to the object’s mass times the force of gravity times the height it’s lifted. The X-Wing scene lets us use this to put a lower limit on Yoda’s peak power output.
First we need to know how heavy the ship was. The X-Wing’s mass has never been canonically established, but its length has—12.5 meters. An F-22 is 19 meters long and weighs 19,700 kg, so scaling down from this gives an estimate for the X-Wing of about 12,000 lbs (5 metric tons).
Next, we need to know how fast it was rising…
We go over footage of the scene (lots of sources on youtube) and we time the X-Wing’s rate of ascent as it was emerging from the water. The front landing strut rises out of the water in about three and a half seconds, and I estimate the strut to be 1.4 meters long (based on a scene in A New Hope where a crew member squeezes past it), which tells us the X-Wing was rising at 0.39 m/s.
Lastly, we need to know the strength of gravity on Dagobah. Wookieepeedia has a catalog of such things and informs us that the surface gravity on Dagobah is 0.9g. Combining this with the X-Wing mass and lift rate gives us our peak power output:
Note that in the experiment it’s advisable to only allow one pupil at a time to run up the stairs. A slope is better if you have one available. I always give a good warning about taking care, wearing sensible footwear etc. If you think your class are likely to be over enthusiastic which would lead to falls and injuries, please skip this. An accessible alternative is to lift a heavy mass through a measured distance with one or two hands, again the mass should be light enough to not cause injury and no pupil should lift a weight higher than their own shoulders. Warn of back damage here.

title: 5  Circular Motion
text:
5.1.1 Definition
Circular motion refers to the movement of an object along the circumference of a circle. It can be uniform (constant speed) or non-uniform (changing speed), but in both cases the direction of motion changes continuously, implying acceleration.


5.1.2 Key Quantities









Quantity
Symbol
Units
Description




Radius
\(r\)
m
Distance from the center to the object


Speed
\(v\)
m/s
Magnitude of the velocity (scalar)


Angular velocity
\(\omega\)
rad/s
Rate of rotation: \(\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}\)


Frequency
\(f\)
Hz
Revolutions per second: \(f = \frac{1}{T}\)


Period
\(T\)
s
Time for one complete revolution


Centripetal acceleration
\(a_c\)
m/s²
Directed toward the center: \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}\)


Centripetal force
\(F_c\)
N
Net force causing circular motion: \(F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}\)





5.1.3 Key Relationships

\(v = \omega r\)
\(a_c = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}\)
\(F_c = ma_c = m\omega^2 r = \frac{mv^2}{r}\)



5.1.4 Direction of Vectors

Velocity is tangential to the circle.
Acceleration and centripetal force point toward the center.
There is no outward force acting on the object (e.g., “centrifugal force” is a fictitious force in an inertial frame).



5.1.5 Examples

A car turning around a bend
A satellite orbiting Earth
An electron moving in a magnetic field
A mass on a string swung in a horizontal circle

Centripetal force is the force that pulls or pushes an object from its straight-line path. It always acts towards the centre of a circle. The centrifugal force is the reaction of this force on the thing doing the pushing or pulling but not on the rotating object itself.
\[
\text{Centripetal force} = \frac{mv^{2}}{R}
\]
where:

\(m\) is the mass of an object moving at a constant speed
\(v\) is the tangential velocity
\(R\) is the radius of the circle round a circle of radius R

title: 5  Circular Motion
text:
5.2 Stories to enrich

5.2.1 Sputnik and the Start of Space Orbits (1957)





When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, it stunned the world — and illustrated circular motion on a planetary scale.
Sputnik stayed in orbit because it was moving sideways fast enough (about 8 km/s) that Earth’s surface curved away beneath it as it “fell.” It didn’t need engines to stay up — just the right speed to balance gravity with inertia, a perfect case of centripetal motion. Circular motion wasn’t just theory anymore — it became the basis of satellite technology, GPS, and global communication.


5.2.2 The World’s Tallest Swing Ride
The StarFlyer ride in Florida lifts passengers nearly 150 meters into the air and spins them around at over 70 km/h.





Despite being “thrown outward,” riders are actually being pulled inward by the tension in the cables — providing the centripetal force. If the cables broke, the rider wouldn’t fly outward — they’d follow a tangent path, showing Newton’s first law in action. It’s thrilling — and a real-life demonstration of circular motion and Newtonian mechanics.


5.2.3 The Spinning Space Station Idea (2001: A Space Odyssey)
In the film 2001: A Space Odyssey, the rotating space station creates artificial gravity by spinning. This isn’t just science fiction — it’s real physics.

In a spinning ring, objects are forced against the outer wall by their inertia. The wall provides the centripetal force, which feels like gravity to the occupants. Engineers have seriously considered building rotating space habitats using this principle to help astronauts stay healthy in zero gravity.

5.3.1 The flying pig…
The theory of circular motion, or indeed, the conical pendulum can be demonstrated wonderfully with this ornithopter toy. The battery drives the mechanism causing the pig to fly in a circle of radius r at a constant speed. It is also a good simulation of the chairs in fairground rides.





The faster the pig the bigger the angle (0) that the string makes with the vertical. Measurements of 0, v, m and r are easy to make, and so the experiment could be used to find the acceleration due to gravity (g).
For a pig of mass \(m\), resolving vertically:
\[ mg = T \cos \theta \]
Resolving horizontally:
\[\frac{mv^{2}}{r} = T \sin \theta\] Therefore: \[ \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \tan \theta = mg \] and so
\[g = \frac{v^{2}}{r} \tan \theta \]

5.3.13 Vertical circles
If a bung is being swung round on a string in a vertical circle at a constant speed the centripetal force must be constant, but because the object has weight (\(mg\)), the string tension vaies.
The tension provides part of the centripetal force as it goes round the top of the loop and provides a supporting force and the centripetal force at the bottom of the loop.
At the bottom of the circle:
\[ T_{string}  - mg = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}\] So.. \[T_{string}  = \frac{mv}{r} + mg \]
At the sides of the circle: \[ T_{string} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}\] At the top of the circle:
\[ T_{string} + mg = mv^{2}/r \]
so
\[ T_{string}  = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} - mg \] #### Bonus story:
An outside loop is an aerobatic maneuver in which an aircraft flies a circular path with the canopy on the outside of the circle, as opposed to a normal or inside loop where the pilot stays on the inside of the circle. In a typical inside loop, positive G-forces push the pilot into the seat, but in an outside loop the pilot experiences negative G-forces that try to pull them out of the seat, placing immense strain on both the pilot’s body and the aircraft.
The outside loop was first successfully performed in 1927 by American pilot Jimmy Doolittle, who flew a Curtiss P-1C Hawk biplane. At the time, many believed the stunt was impossible or suicidal due to the extreme negative G-forces involved, but Doolittle’s achievement marked a milestone in aviation history, proving both the strength of modern aircraft and the resilience of skilled pilots. Outside loops are particularly challenging because the negative G-forces, which can reach minus three to minus five G or more, can cause great discomfort, vision problems such as red-out, or even loss of consciousness.
The aircraft itself must be strong enough to withstand these forces without structural failure, and the pilot must exert precise control to avoid dangerous spins or crashes. Today, outside loops are a standard element in aerobatic competitions and displays, but they remain a demanding test of both machine and pilot, showcasing advances in aircraft engineering and human endurance.


5.3.14 Toy cars, loop the loop
Toy cars on a plastic track can be used to demonstrate a number of ideas in mechanics. If the track can be bent into a vertical circle then loop the loop experiments can be performed.
The problem of “will it make it round?” can be approached as follows:
The Centripetal force is provided by a combination of the reaction of the track (R) and the force of gravity (mg). At the top of the path the car can travel at its minimum speed since the centripetal force can be provided by gravity alone.
The minimum reaction occurs at the top of the path where:
\[\frac{mv_{t}^{2}}{r} = mg \] So \[
v_{t} = \sqrt{gr}
\] where: - \(r\) is the radius of the loop. - \(v_t\) is the velocity at the top of the loop.
so far we have worked out the minimum speed that maintains contact with the loop. To work out the minimum entry speed (\(v_e\)) we need to use conservation of energy:
Assuming the car just makes it up a loop of height \(2r\) (where \(r\) is the radius of the loop), the gain in GPE is \(mgh\) so the minimum speed is ;
\[ mg \times 2r = 1/2mv_{e}^{2} + 1/2mv_{t}^{2}\] substituting \(v_{t}^{2} = gr\) \[
mg \times 2r = 1/2mv_{e}^{2} + 1/2mgr
\] Cancel \(m\);
\[
g \times 2r = 1/2v_{e}^{2} + 1/2gr
\]
so \[
v_{e} = \sqrt{5gr}\]

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.1 Basic Theory
The size of a force is measured in units called Newtons (N). You can get a rough idea of a force’s size by thinking about the pull of the Earth on us.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.1.1 Mass
This is the amount of stuff (matter) in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg) and is always the same wherever the object is. The only way to change the mass of something is to chip a bit off! (Ignoring relativistic effects of course.)


6.1.2 Weight
The force of attraction of the Earth on us is our WEIGHT. The more massive we are the bigger is the force of attraction and the bigger is our weight. This also gives us a rough definition of the Newton. A Newton is the pull of the Earth on about 100 g. The pull of the Earth on 1 kg is about 10 N.


6.1.3 Newton’s First Law (Law of Inertia)

An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force.
This means: \[
\text{If } \sum \vec{F} = 0, \quad \vec{v} = \text{constant}
\]



6.1.4 Newton’s Second Law (Law of Acceleration)

The acceleration \(\vec{a}\) of an object is proportional to the net force \(\sum \vec{F}\) acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass \(m\): \[
\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a}
\]
This law quantifies how forces change motion.



6.1.5 Newton’s Third Law (Action-Reaction)

For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force: \[
\vec{F}_{\text{AB}} = - \vec{F}_{\text{BA}}
\]
Forces always come in pairs acting on two different objects.



6.1.6 Implications and Applications

Objects at rest or moving uniformly have zero net force.
To change motion, a force must be applied.
The same magnitude force applied to different masses results in different accelerations.
Reaction forces explain propulsion, walking, rocket thrust, etc.



6.1.7 Summary Table








Law
Statement
Formula




First Law
Object remains in uniform motion unless force acts
\(\sum \vec{F} = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{v} = \text{constant}\)


Second Law
Force causes acceleration proportional to mass
\(\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a}\)


Third Law
Action and reaction forces are equal and opposite
\(\vec{F}_{\text{AB}} = -\vec{F}_{\text{BA}}\)



To change the way an object is moving you need a force.
This force can either:

speed up the object, like a sprinter at the start of a race or..
slow down the object, like a motorbike slowing down as it approaches a red traffic signal or..
change the direction in which the object is moving, like a car turning a corner

Newton’s three laws of motion may be summarised as follows:

A body remains at rest or in a state of uniform motion unless acted on by a force. What is still stays still and what is moving stays moving at a steady speed in a straight line unless a force acts on it.
The resultant force on a body causes an acceleration which depends on both the size of the force and the mass of the body, i.e. \(\text{Force} = \text{Mass} \times  \text{Acceleration}\)
If a force acts on one body an equal and opposite force acts on another body.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.2 Stories to enrich

6.2.1 Newton’s Apple: A Story of Stillness and Insight
The famous apple story is actually true, at least according to the Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton’s Life, written by William Stukeley, an archaeologist and one of Newton’s first biographers. Stukeley records his conversation with Newton as follows:

“After dinner, the weather being warm, we went into the garden and drank tea, under the shade of some apple trees…he told me, he was just in the same situation, as when formerly, the notion of gravitation came into his mind. It was occasion’d by the fall of an apple, as he sat in contemplative mood. Why should that apple always descend perpendicularly to the ground, thought he to himself…”

you can read the book, published in 1752 here:





Rather brilliantly, a piece of Newton’s apple tree was taken into space by British-born astronaut Piers Sellers as part of the 350 year celebrations.


6.2.2 The Horse and Cart Debate That Divided Philosophers
When Newton’s Third Law was proposed, critics raised a question: if a horse pulls on a cart, and the cart pulls back equally, how does anything move? This wasn’t just a joke—it sparked a genuine puzzle. The answer lies in the interaction with the ground: the horse pushes backward on the Earth, which pushes it forward. Newton’s Third Law is not a paradox, but a law of equal pairs, not cancellation. This insight became essential in understanding propulsion—whether walking, rowing, or spaceflight.
Reflection: How can a misunderstanding of Newton’s First and Third Law lead to confusion in everyday reasoning?


6.2.3 The Duel of Masks and the Vacuum Chamber
In 1654, Otto von Guericke, mayor of Magdeburg, staged a spectacle to demonstrate the force of air pressure and inertia. He created two large copper hemispheres, evacuated the air from within, and then hitched teams of horses to either side. Despite their efforts, the hemispheres could not be pulled apart. What amazed the public was not just the demonstration of pressure, but the indirect implication of Newton’s First Law: the air (or lack of it) was exerting a massive force, even though nothing visible was “pushing.”



The original Magdeburg hemispheres.




6.2.4 The Nuclear Cannon
One of the fastest moving man-made objects ever fired was not a specially designed projectile so much as a manhole cover. The 1957 Pascal-B nuclear test in Nevada was an underground nuclear detonation. The 900 kg steel plate that capped the well down to the explosive was blown off the top of a test shaft so rapidly that the high-speed camera footage of the incident captured the manhole cover in just one frame. Working from the framerate we conclude that the speed must have been more than 66 km/s. The plate was never found, and although the plate exceeded Earth’s escape velocity, it is most likely to have been vaporised by compression heating on it’s way through the atmosphere.

6.3 Practical work and Demos

6.3.1 Newton’s 2nd Law experiment
The classic physics experiment is the N2 experiment in which a small trolley which is accelerated along a friction-compensated track by a number of small masses (washers are ideal) tied to a thread which is fixed to the trolley after passing over a pulley.The friction compensated track removes the effect of the work done against friction by the cart and is achieved by simply tilting the track until the cart, pushed lightly, continues to roll down the slope at steady speed.
We usually use lightgates to measure the acceleration by measuring the difference in velocity at two points a measured time interval apart. You can also directly measure acceleration with lightgates or accelerometers (phyphox is great for this).
If you don’t have any such technology available, or if you want to do it a bit differently you can time the trolley from a standing start over a known distance and then use: \[s = ut + 0.5 at^{2}\]
where:

\(t\) is the time period measured
\(u\) is the initial velocity (0)
\(a\) is the acceleration to be calculated
\(s\) is the measured distance

to calculate the average acceleration. Another variation with a speed only sensor would be to use: \[v^{2}=u^{2} + 2as\]
where:

\(v\) is the final velocity measured
\(u\) is the initial velocity (0)
\(a\) is the acceleration to be calculated
\(s\) is the measured distance

Despite being the experiment, an awful lot of students conduct it incorrectly. In order to get meaningful results it’s important to ensure mass being accelerated is constant. This means it’s critical to transfer the weights from the trolley to the accelerating mass or vice versa. In other words, when you plot graphs of acceleration against force The total mass of all objects accelerating is the constant gradient.
One of the odd issues with this experiment that you can get round with modern technology is that we take the accelerating force as mg - using the very law that we are trying to verify. If you have accelerometer and force meter available you can measure the quantities directly. Plotting the values against each other should validate N2 although if you have a very able class you could use an elastic attachment from the force meter to the car and have some fun…
Theory: \[ \text{Accelerating force (F)}  = mg = \text{ Total mass }\times \text{ acceleration} = (M+m)a\] Where:

\(m\) is the mass of the accelerating mass acting on the trolley and
\(M\) is the total mass of the trolley and the accelerating mass.

When a spacecraft approaches a planet that is moving through space the spacecraft experiences a sling shot effect due to the motion of the planet. title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.4 1st law & 3rd law pairs.
A common misconception arises when people confuse Newton’s First Law with the action-reaction pairs described in Newton’s Third Law. Newton’s First Law states that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force, emphasizing how motion changes only when forces are unbalanced. In contrast, Newton’s Third Law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction — forces always come in pairs acting on different objects. The confusion often lies in thinking that these action-reaction forces cancel each other out and thus prevent motion, but this is incorrect because they act on separate bodies. For example, when you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you equally, but these forces act on different objects and do not cancel in the sense of preventing movement altogether; whether motion occurs depends on other forces acting on each object. Understanding that First Law forces sum on a single object while Third Law pairs act on different objects is key to resolving this confusion.

title: 6  Forces and Newton’s Laws
text:
6.5 Rockets
The propulsion systems of rockets depend on the laws of momentum conservation and are well explained by the three newtonian laws. For a solid or liquid fuel rocket, the greater the velocity of the exhaust gases the greater is their momentum and hence the greater the momentum of the rocket.
When fuel burns in the rocket’s combustion chamber it creates hot, high-pressure gas made of billions of fast-moving particles. These particles zoom around randomly and collide with the chamber walls in all directions.Particles hit all the walls equally (left, right, top, bottom). Were these forces to balance, as they do perpendicular to the rocket, there’d be no resultant force/
At the nozzle opening however, the gas particles escape out the nozzle at high speed. This means that there’s fewer collisions on the nozzle side’s wall compared to the front wall. This imbalance of pressure inside the chamber creates a net force pushing the rocket forward.

6.5.1 Calculating Rocket Velocity with Changing Mass, Gravity, and Air Resistance
Calculating the velocity of a rocket properly is mathematically demanding - Let’s take a very crude model as an example:

Changing mass
Gravity
Air resistance (drag)


1. Ideal Rocket Equation (No Air Resistance)
In space (no gravity, no air), we start with the Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation:
\[
\Delta v = v_e \ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)
\]
where:

\(\Delta v\) = change in velocity

\(v_e\) = exhaust velocity of the gases

\(m_0\) = initial mass (rocket + fuel)

\(m_f\) = final mass (after fuel burned)



2. Including Gravity
If launching vertically near Earth, gravity subtracts velocity, note that this assumes that we dont stray far enough to consider Earth’s gravitational field as anything other than uniform:
\[
v(t) = v_e \ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m(t)}\right) - g \, t
\]
where \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity (≈ 9.81 m/s²).


3. Air Resistance (Drag)
Drag force is given by:
\[
F_{\text{drag}} = \frac{1}{2} \, \rho \, v^2 \, C_D \, A
\]
where:

\(\rho\) = air density

\(v\) = rocket velocity

\(C_D\) = drag coefficient (shape-dependent)

\(A\) = cross-sectional area

Drag reduces the rocket’s net acceleration:
\[
a = \frac{T - F_{\text{drag}} - m \, g}{m}
\]
where:

\(T\) = thrust force

\(m\) = rocket mass at time \(t\)

Since \(m\) changes as fuel burns, we get a differential equation:
\[
m(t) \, \frac{dv}{dt}
=
T
-
\frac{1}{2} \, \rho \, v^2 \, C_D \, A
-
m(t) \, g
\]


4. Full Differential Equation
We can express the velocity change as:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{dv}{dt}
=
\frac{T}{m(t)}
-
\frac{1}{2} \frac{\rho \, v^2 \, C_D \, A}{m(t)}
-
g
}
\]
and:
\[
m(t) = m_0 - \dot{m} \cdot t
\]
where \(\dot{m}\) is the mass flow rate (fuel used per second).
Because drag depends on \(v\), and \(\rho\) changes with altitude, we usually solve this numerically.
